title: Multiplatform Dependencies
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of multiplatform dependencies using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates multiplatform dependencies.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Multiplatform Dependencies** as part of **Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform**. Kotlin Multiplatform organizes shared logic and target-specific implementations through source sets; only APIs available for every configured target belong in common code. Use the subtopics—Platform-Compatible Libraries, Source-Set Dependency Configuration, Managing Library Compatibility—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Multiplatform work succeeds when shared code depends only on common APIs and platform-specific code is isolated behind deliberate interfaces.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Kotlin Multiplatform organizes shared logic and target-specific implementations through source sets; only APIs available for every configured target belong in common code.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with platform-compatible libraries. Then compare it with source-set dependency configuration. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Platform-Compatible Libraries
items.text: Platform-Compatible Libraries is one part of multiplatform dependencies. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Source-Set Dependency Configuration
items.text: Source-Set Dependency Configuration is best learned by tracing a small collection before and after the operation. Check ordering, duplicate handling, empty inputs, and whether the API returns a new value or mutates a mutable receiver.

items.title: Managing Library Compatibility
items.text: Managing Library Compatibility means checking the boundary between the language feature and its compiler, runtime, plugin, library, or target version. Pin the versions used by the project and verify documented support before depending on the behavior.

content_blocks.code:
data class Greeting(val text: String)

fun greetingFor(name: String): Greeting = Greeting("Hello, $name")

fun main() = println(greetingFor("Kotlin").text)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run inside a Kotlin Multiplatform project with the target toolchains installed; common and platform-specific source sets have different APIs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Multiplatform Dependencies removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.text: Check one edge case and the official reference for the selected Kotlin/runtime version.
